entries.ce3aef95ddef4811c3e95d481eae60d17b36483a: <div sID="gen16187" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="33" osisID="Isa.33" sID="Isa.33"/> <div eID="gen16187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16188" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16189" type="x-p"/> This chapter relates to the same events as the foregoing chapter, the distress of Judah and Jerusalem by Sennacherib's invasion and their deliverance out of that distress by the destruction of the Assyrian army. These are intermixed in the prophecy, in the way of a Pindaric. Observe, I. The great distress that Judah and Jerusalem should then be brought into, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.7-Isa.33.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. II. The particular frights which the sinners in Zion should then be in, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.13-Isa.33.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. III. The prayers of good people to God in this distress, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">ver. 2</reference>. IV. The holy security which they should enjoy in the midst of this trouble, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15-Isa.33.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. V. The destruction of the army of the Assyrians (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.1-Isa.33.3">ver. 1-3</reference>), in which God would be greatly glorified, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">ver. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10-Isa.33.12">10-12</reference>. VI. The enriching of the Jews with the spoil of the Assyrian camp, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.23">23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">24</reference>. VII. The happy settlement of Jerusalem, and the Jewish state, upon this. Religion shall be uppermost (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.6">ver. 6</reference>), and their civil state shall flourish, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.17-Isa.33.22">ver. 17-22</reference>. This was soon fulfilled, but is written for our learning.
entries.259ee96a93f305deef2d0f792a62937a798718ca: <div eID="gen16189" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16188" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Assyria Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16190" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to thee that spoilest, and thou <hi type="italic">wast</hi> not spoiled; and dealest treacherously, and they dealt not treacherously with thee! when thou shalt cease to spoil, thou shalt be spoiled; <hi type="italic">and</hi> when thou shalt make an end to deal treacherously, they shall deal treacherously with thee.   2 <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , be gracious unto us; we have waited for thee: be thou their arm every morning, our salvation also in the time of trouble. <hi type="super">3</hi> At the noise of the tumult the people fled; at the lifting up of thyself the nations were scattered. <hi type="super">4</hi> And your spoil shall be gathered <hi type="italic">like</hi> the gathering of the caterpillar: as the running to and fro of locusts shall he run upon them. <hi type="super">5</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is exalted; for he dwelleth on high: he hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. <hi type="super">6</hi> And wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, <hi type="italic">and</hi> strength of salvation: the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> his treasure. <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, their valiant ones shall cry without: the ambassadors of peace shall weep bitterly. <hi type="super">8</hi> The highways lie waste, the wayfaring man ceaseth: he hath broken the covenant, he hath despised the cities, he regardeth no man. <hi type="super">9</hi> The earth mourneth <hi type="italic">and</hi> languisheth: Lebanon is ashamed <hi type="italic">and</hi> hewn down: Sharon is like a wilderness; and Bashan and Carmel shake off <hi type="italic">their fruits.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> Now will I rise, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; now will I be exalted; now will I lift up myself. <hi type="super">11</hi> Ye shall conceive chaff, ye shall bring forth stubble: your breath, <hi type="italic">as</hi> fire, shall devour you. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the people shall be <hi type="italic">as</hi> the burnings of lime: <hi type="italic">as</hi> thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire. <div eID="gen16190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16191" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen16191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16192" type="x-p"/> I. The proud and false Assyrian justly reckoned with for all his fraud and violence, and laid under a woe, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">v. 1</reference>. Observe, 1. The sin which the enemy had been guilty of. He had spoiled the people of God, and made a prey of them, and herein had broken his treaty of peace with them, and dealt treacherously. Truth and mercy are two such sacred things, and have so much of God in them, that those cannot but be under the wrath of God that make conscience of neither, but are perfectly lost to both, that care not what mischief they do, what spoil they make, what dissimulations they are guilty of, nor what solemn engagements they violate, to compass their own wicked designs. Bloody and deceitful men are the worst of men. 2. The aggravation of this sin. He spoiled those that had never done him any injury and that he had no pretence to quarrel with, and dealt treacherously with those that had always dealt faithfully with him. Note, The less provocation we have from men to do a wrong thing the more provocation we give to God by doing it. 3. The punishment he should fall under for this sin. He that spoiled the cities of Judah shall have his own army destroyed by an angel and his camp plundered by those whom he had made a prey of. The Chaldeans shall deal treacherously with the Assyrians and revolt from them. Two of Sennacherib's own sons shall deal treacherously with him and basely murder him at his devotions. Note, The righteous God often pays sinners in their own coin. <hi type="italic">He that leads into captivity shall go into captivity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">xviii. 6</reference>. 4. The time when he shall be thus dealt with. When he shall <hi type="italic">make an end to spoil, and to deal treacherously,</hi> not by repentance and reformation, which might prevent his ruin (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Dan. iv. 27</reference>), but when he shall have done his worst, when he shall have gone as far as God would permit him to go, to the utmost of his tether, then the cup of trembling shall be put into his hand. When he shall have arrived at his full stature in impiety, shall have filled up the measure of his iniquity, then all shall be called over again. When he has done God will begin, for his day is coming. <div eID="gen16192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16193" type="x-p"/> II. The praying people of God earnest at the throne of grace for mercy for the land now in its distress (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Lord! be merciful to us.</hi> Men are cruel; be thou gracious. We have deserved thy wrath, but we entreat thy favour; and, if we may find the propitious to us, we are happy; the trouble we are in cannot hurt us, shall not ruin us. It is in vain to expect relief from creatures; we have no confidence in the Egyptians, but <hi type="italic">we have waited for thee</hi> only, resolving to submit to thee, whatever the issue of the trouble be, and hoping that it shall be a comfortable issue." Those that by faith humbly wait for God shall certainly find him gracious to them. They prayed, 1. For those that were employed in military services for them: "<hi type="italic">Be thou their arm every morning.</hi> Hezekiah, and his princes, and all the men of war, need continual supplies of strength and courage from thee; supply their need therefore, and be to them a God all-sufficient. Every morning, when they go forth upon the business of the day, and perhaps have new work to do and new difficulties to encounter, let them be afresh animated and invigorated, and, <hi type="italic">as the day, so let the strength be.</hi>" In our spiritual warfare our own hands are not sufficient for us, nor can we bring any thing to pass unless God not only strengthen our arms (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Gen. xlix. 24</reference>), but be himself our arm; so entirely do we depend upon him as our arm every morning, so constantly do we depend upon his power, as well as his compassions, which are new every morning, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.23">Lam. iii. 23</reference>. If God leaves us to ourselves any morning, we are undone; we must therefore every morning commit ourselves to him, and go forth in his strength to do the work of the day in its day. 2. For the body of the people: "<hi type="italic">Be thou our salvation also in the time of trouble,</hi> ours who sit still, and do not venture into the high places of the field." They depend upon God not only as their Saviour, to work deliverance for them, but as their salvation itself; for, whatever becomes of their secular interests, they will reckon themselves safe and saved if they have him for their God. If he undertake to be their Saviour, he will be their salvation; for <hi type="italic">as for God his work is perfect.</hi> Some read it thus: "<hi type="italic">Thou who wast their arm every morning,</hi> who wast the continual strength and help of our fathers before us, <hi type="italic">be thou our salvation also in time of trouble.</hi> Help us as thou helpedst them; <hi type="italic">they looked unto thee and were lightened</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.5">Ps. xxxiv. 5</reference>); let us then not walk in darkness." <div eID="gen16193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16194" type="x-p"/> III. The Assyrian army ruined and their camp made a rich but cheap and easy prey to Judah and Jerusalem. No sooner is the prayer made (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">v. 2</reference>) than it is answered (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">v. 3</reference>), nay, it is outdone. They prayed that God would save them from their enemies; but he did more than that; he gave them victory over their enemies and abundant cause to triumph; for, 1. The strength of the Assyrian camp was broken (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">v. 3</reference>) when the destroying angel slew so many thousands of them: <hi type="italic">At the noise of the tumult,</hi> of the shrieks of the dying men (who, we may suppose, did not die silently), the rest of <hi type="italic">the people fled,</hi> and shifted every one for his own safety. When God did thus lift up himself the several nations, or clans, of which the army was composed, were scattered. It was time to stir when such an unprecedented plague broke out among them. When God arises his enemies are scattered, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.1">Ps. lxviii. 1</reference>. 2. The spoil of the Assyrian camp is seized, by way of reprisal, for all the desolations of the defenced cities of Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Your spoil shall be gathered</hi> by the inhabitants of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">like the gathering of the caterpillar,</hi> and <hi type="italic">as the running to and fro of locusts,</hi> that is, the spoilers shall as easily and as quickly make themselves masters of the riches of the Assyrians as a host of caterpillars, or locusts, make a field, or a tree, bare. Thus <hi type="italic">the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just</hi> and Israel is enriched with the spoil of the Egyptians. Some make the Assyrians to be the caterpillars and locusts, which, when they are killed, are gathered together in heaps, as the frogs of Egypt, and are run upon, and trodden to dirt. <div eID="gen16194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16195" type="x-p"/> IV. God and his Israel glorified and exalted hereby. When the spoil of the enemy is thus gathered, 1. God will have the praise of it (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is exalted.</hi> It is his honour thus to abase proud men, and hide them in the dust, together; thus he magnifies his own name, and his people give him the glory of it, as Israel when the Egyptians were drowned, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.1-Exod.15.2">Exod. xv. 1, 2</reference>, &c. He is exalted as one that dwells on high, out of the reach of their blasphemies, and that has an over-ruling power over them, and wherein they deal proudly delights to show himself above them-that does what he will, and they cannot resist him. 2. His people will have the blessing of it. When God lifts up himself to scatter the nations that are in confederacy against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">v. 3</reference>) then, as a preparative for that, or as the fruit and product of it, <hi type="italic">he has filled Zion with judgment and righteousness,</hi> not only with a sense of justice, but with a zeal for it and a universal care that it be duly administered. It shall again be called, <hi type="italic">The city of righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">ch. i. 26</reference>. In this the grace of God is exalted, as much as his providence was in the destruction of the Assyrian army. We may conclude God has mercy in store for a people when he fills them with judgment and righteousness, when all sorts of people, and all their actions and affairs, are governed by them, and they are so full of them that no other considerations can crowd in to sway them against these. Hezekiah and his people are encouraged (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.6">v. 6</reference>) with an assurance that God would stand by them in their distress. Here is, (1.) A gracious promise of God for them to stay themselves upon: <hi type="italic">Wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and strength of salvation.</hi> Here is a desirable end proposed, and that is <hi type="italic">the stability of our times,</hi> that things be not disturbed and unhinged at home, and the <hi type="italic">strength of salvation,</hi> deliverance from, and success against, enemies abroad. The salvation that God ordains for his people has strength in it; it is a horn of salvation. And here are the way and means for obtaining this end—<hi type="italic">wisdom and knowledge,</hi> not only piety, but prudence. That is it which, by the blessing of God, will be the <hi type="italic">stability of our times and the strength of salvation,</hi> that wisdom which is first pure, then peaceable, and which sacrifices private interests to a public good; such prudence as this will establish truth and peace, and fortify the bulwarks in defence of them. (2.) A pious maxim of state for Hezekiah and his people to govern themselves by: <hi type="italic">The fear of the Lord is his treasure.</hi> It is God's treasure in the world, from which he receives his tribute; or, rather, it is the prince's treasure. A good prince accounts it so (that wisdom is better than gold) and he shall find it so. Note, True religion is the true treasure of any prince or people; it denominates them rich. Those places that have plenty of Bibles, and ministers, and serious good people, are really rich; and it contributes to that which makes a nation rich in this world. It is therefore the interest of a people to support religion among them and to take heed of every thing that threatens to hinder it. <div eID="gen16195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16196" type="x-p"/> V. The great distress that Jerusalem was brought into described, that those who believed the prophet might know beforehand what troubles were coming and might provide accordingly, and that when the foregoing promise of their deliverance should have its accomplishment the remembrance of the extremity of their case might help to magnify God in it and make them the more thankful, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.7-Isa.33.9">v. 7-9</reference>. It is here foretold, 1. That the enemy would be very insolent and abusive and there would be no dealing with him, either by treaties of peace (<hi type="italic">for he has broken the covenant</hi> without any hesitation, as if it were below him to be a servant to his word), or by the preparations of war, for <hi type="italic">he has despised the cities;</hi> he scorns to take notice either of their appeals to justice or of their petitions for mercy. He makes himself master of them so easily (though they are called <hi type="italic">fenced cities</hi>), and meets with so little resistance, that he despises them, and has no relentings when he puts all to the sword; for he regards no man, has no pity or concern, no, not for those that he is under particular obligations to. He neither fears God nor regards man, but is haughty and imperious to every one. There are those that take a pride in trampling upon all mankind, and have neither veneration for the honourable nor compassion for the miserable. 2. That therefore he would not be brought to any terms of reconciliation: <hi type="italic">The valiant ones of Jerusalem,</hi> being unable to make their parts good with him, must be contentedly run down with noise and insolence, which will make them cry without, because they cannot serve their country as they might have done against a fair adversary. <hi type="italic">The ambassadors</hi> sent by Hezekiah to treat <hi type="italic">of peace,</hi> finding him so haughty and unmanageable, <hi type="italic">shall weep bitterly</hi> for vexation at the disappointment they had met with in their negotiations; they shall weep like children, as despairing to find out any expedient to pacify him. 3. That the country should be made quite desolate for a time by his army. (1.) No man durst travel the roads; so that a stop was put to trade and commerce, and (which was worse) no man could safely go up to Jerusalem, to keep the solemn feasts: <hi type="italic">The highways lie waste.</hi> While the fields lie waste, trodden like the highways, the highways lie waste, untrodden like the fields, for <hi type="italic">the traveller ceases.</hi> (2.) No man had any profit from the grounds, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">v. 9</reference>. The earth used to rejoice in its own productions for the service of God's Israel, but now the enemies of Israel eat them up, or tread them down: it <hi type="italic">mourns and languishes;</hi> the country looks melancholy and the country people have misery in their countenances, wanting necessary food for themselves and their families; the wonted joy of harvest is turned into lamentation, so withering and uncertain are all worldly joys. The desolation is universal. That part of the country which belonged to the ten tribes was already laid waste: "<hi type="italic">Lebanon</hi> famed for cedars, <hi type="italic">Sharon</hi> for roses, <hi type="italic">Bashan</hi> for cattle, <hi type="italic">Carmel</hi> for corn, all very fruitful, have now become like wildernesses, <hi type="italic">are ashamed</hi> to be called by their old names, they are so unlike what they were. They <hi type="italic">shake off their fruits</hi> before their time into the hand of the spoiler, which used to be gathered seasonably by the hand of the owner." <div eID="gen16196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16197" type="x-p"/> VI. God appearing, at length, in his glory against his proud invader, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10">v. 10-12</reference>. When things are brought thus to the last extremity, 1. God will magnify himself. He had seemed to sit by as an unconcerned spectator: "But <hi type="italic">now will I arise, saith the Lord;</hi> now will I appear and act, and therein I will be not only evidenced, but exalted." He will not only demonstrate that there is a God that judges in the earth, but that he is God over all, and higher than the highest. "Now <hi type="italic">will I lift up myself,</hi> will prepare for action, will act vigorously, and will be glorified in it." God's time to appear for his people is when their affairs are reduced to the lowest ebb, <hi type="italic">when their strength is gone and there is none shut up nor left,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deut. xxxii. 36</reference>. When all other helpers fail, then is God's time to help. 2. He will bring down the Assyrian: "You, O Assyrians! are big with hopes that you shall have all the wealth of Jerusalem for your own, and are in pain till it be so; but all your hopes shall come to nothing: <hi type="italic">You shall conceive chaff, and bring forth stubble,</hi> which is not only worthless and good for nothing, but combustible and proper fuel for the fire, which it cannot escape, when <hi type="italic">your</hi> own <hi type="italic">breath as fire shall devour you,</hi> that is, the breath of God's wrath, provoked against you by the breath of your sins—your malignant breath, the threatenings and slaughter you breathe out against the people of God, this shall devour you, and your blasphemous breath against God and his name." God would make their own tongues to fall upon them, and their own breath to blow the fire that should consume them; and then no wonder that the people are <hi type="italic">as the burnings of lime</hi> in a lime-kiln, all on fire together, and <hi type="italic">as thorns cut up,</hi> which are dried and withered, and therefore easily take fire and are soon burnt up. Such was the destruction of the Assyrian army; it was like the burning up of thorns, which can well be spared, or the burning of lime, which makes it good for something. The burning of that army enlightened the world with the knowledge of God's power and made his name shine brightly.
entries.61513f7822bf13b454795adc0df7cae65766552e: <div eID="gen16197" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Forebodings of Hypocrites; Encouragement to God's People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16198" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Hear, ye <hi type="italic">that are</hi> far off, what I have done; and, ye <hi type="italic">that are</hi> near, acknowledge my might. <hi type="super">14</hi> The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings? <hi type="super">15</hi> He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes, that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil; <hi type="super">16</hi> He shall dwell on high: his place of defence <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the munitions of rocks: bread shall be given him; his waters <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> sure. <hi type="super">17</hi> Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off. <hi type="super">18</hi> Thine heart shall meditate terror. Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the scribe? where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the receiver? where <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that counted the towers? <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, <hi type="italic">that thou canst</hi> not understand. <hi type="super">20</hi> Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken. <hi type="super">21</hi> But there the glorious <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">will be</hi> unto us a place of broad rivers <hi type="italic">and</hi> streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby. <hi type="super">22</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> our judge, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> our lawgiver, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> our king; he will save us. <hi type="super">23</hi> Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail: then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick: the people that dwell therein <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> forgiven <hi type="italic">their</hi> iniquity. <div eID="gen16198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16199" type="x-p"/> Here is a preface that commands attention; and it is fit that all should attend, both near and afar off, to what God says and does (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear, you that are afar off,</hi> whether in place or time. Let distant regions and future ages hear what God has done. They do so; they will do so from the scripture, with as much assurance as those that were near, the neighbouring nations and those that lived at that time. But whoever hears what God has done, whether near or afar off, let them acknowledge his might, that it is irresistible, and that he can do every thing. Those are very stupid who hear what God has done and yet will not acknowledge his might. Now what is it that God has done which we must take notice of, and in which we must acknowledge his might? <div eID="gen16199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16200" type="x-p"/> I. He has struck a terror upon the sinners in Zion (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fearfulness has surprised the hypocrites.</hi> There are sinners in Zion, hypocrites, that enjoy Zion's privileges and concur in Zion's services, but their hearts are not right in the sight of God; they keep up secret haunts of sin under the cloak of a visible profession, which convicts them of hypocrisy. Sinners in Zion will have a great deal to answer for above other sinners; and their place in Zion will be so far from being their security that it will aggravate both their sin and their punishment. Now those sinners in Zion, though always subject to secret frights and terrors, were struck with a more than ordinary consternation from the convictions of their own consciences. 1. When they saw the Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem, and ready to set fire to it and lay it in ashes, and burn the wasps in the nest. Finding they could not make their escape to Egypt, as some had done, and distrusting the promises God had made by his prophets that he would deliver them, they were at their wits' end, and ran about like men distracted, crying, "<hi type="italic">Who among us shall dwell with devouring fire?</hi> Let us therefore abandon the city, and shift for ourselves elsewhere; one had as good live in everlasting burnings as live here." <hi type="italic">Who will stand up for us against this devouring fire?</hi> so some read it. See here how the sinners in Zion are affected when the judgments of God are abroad; while they were only threatened they slighted them and made nothing of them; but, when they come to be executed, they run into the other extreme, then they magnify them, and make the worst of them; they call them <hi type="italic">devouring fire</hi> and <hi type="italic">everlasting burnings,</hi> and despair of relief and succour. Those that rebel against the commands of the word cannot take the comforts of it in a time of need. Or, rather, 2. When they saw the Assyrian army destroyed; for the destruction of that is the fire spoken of immediately before, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.11-Isa.33.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. When the sinners in Zion saw what dreadful execution the wrath of God made they were in a great fright, being conscious to themselves that they had provoked this God by their secretly worshipping other gods; and therefore they cry out, <hi type="italic">Who among us shall dwell with this devouring fire,</hi> before which so vast an army is as thorns? <hi type="italic">Who among us shall dwell with</hi> these <hi type="italic">everlasting burnings,</hi> which have made the Assyrians <hi type="italic">as the burnings of lime?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.12">v. 12</reference>. Thus they said, or should have said. Note, God's judgments upon the enemies of Zion should strike a terror upon the sinners in Zion, nay, David himself trembles at them, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.120">Ps. cxix. 120</reference>. God himself is this devouring fire, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.29">Heb. xii. 29</reference>. Who is able to stand before him? <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.20">1 Sam. vi. 20</reference>. His wrath will burn those everlastingly that have made themselves fuel for it. It is a fire that shall never be quenched, nor will ever go out of itself; for it is the wrath of an everlasting God preying upon the conscience of an immortal soul. Nor can the most daring sinners bear up against it, so as to bear either the execution of it or the fearful expectation of it. Let this awaken us all to flee from the wrath to come, by fleeing to Christ as our refuge. <div eID="gen16200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16201" type="x-p"/> II. He has graciously provided for the security of his people that trust in him: <hi type="italic">Hear this, and acknowledge his</hi> power in making those that <hi type="italic">walk righteously,</hi> and <hi type="italic">speak uprightly,</hi> to <hi type="italic">dwell on high,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15-Isa.33.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. We have here, <div eID="gen16201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16202" type="x-p"/> 1. The good man's character, which he preserves even in times of common iniquity, in divers instances. (1.) He walks righteously. In the whole course of his conversation he acts by rules of equity, and makes conscience of rendering to all their due, to God his due, as well as to men theirs. His walk is righteousness itself; he would not for a world wilfully do an unjust thing. (2.) He speaks uprightly, <hi type="italic">uprightnesses</hi> (so the word is); he speaks what is true and right, and with an honest intention. He cannot think one thing and speak another, nor look one way and row another. His word is to him as sacred as his oath, and is not yea and nay. (3.) He is so far from coveting ill-gotten gain that he despises it. He thinks it a mean and sordid thing, and unbecoming a man of honour, to enrich himself by any hardship put upon his neighbour. He scorns to do a wrong thing, nay, to do a severe thing, though he might get by it. He does not over-value gain itself, and therefore easily abhors the gain that is not honestly come by. (4.) If he have a bribe at any time thrust into his hand, to pervert justice, <hi type="italic">he shakes his hands from holding</hi> it, with the utmost detestation, taking it as an affront to have it offered him. (5.) <hi type="italic">He stops his ears from hearing</hi> any thing that tends to cruelty or bloodshed, or any suggestions stirring him up to revenge, <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job xxxi. 31</reference>. He turns a deaf ear to those that delight in war and entice him to <hi type="italic">cast in his lot among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.14">Prov. i. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">16</reference>. (6.) He <hi type="italic">shuts his eyes from seeing evil.</hi> He has such an abhorrence of sin that he cannot bear to see others commit it, and does himself watch against all the occasions of it. Those that would preserve the purity of their souls must keep a strict guard upon the senses of their bodies, must stop their ears to temptations, and turn away their eyes from beholding vanity. <div eID="gen16202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16203" type="x-p"/> 2. The good man's comfort, which he may preserve even in times of common calamity, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">v. 16</reference>. (1.) He shall be safe; he shall escape the devouring fire and the everlasting burnings; he shall have access to, and communion with, that God who is a devouring fire, but shall be to him a rejoicing light. And, as to present troubles, <hi type="italic">he shall dwell on high,</hi> out of the reach of them, nay, out of the hearing of the noise of them; he shall not be really harmed by them, nay, he shall not be greatly frightened at them: <hi type="italic">The floods of great waters shall not come nigh him;</hi> or, if they should attack him, <hi type="italic">his place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks,</hi> strong and impregnable, fortified by nature as well as art. The divine power will keep him safe, and his faith in that power will keep him easy. God, the rock of ages, will be his high tower. (2.) He shall be supplied; he shall want nothing that is necessary for him: <hi type="italic">Bread shall be given him,</hi> even when the siege is straitest and provisions are cut off; and <hi type="italic">his waters shall be sure,</hi> that is, he shall be sure of the continuance of them, so that he shall not drink his water by measure and with astonishment. Those that fear the Lord shall not want any thing that is good for them. <div eID="gen16203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16204" type="x-p"/> III. He will protect Jerusalem, and deliver it out of the hands of the invaders. This storm that threatened them should blow over, and they should enjoy a prosperous state again. Many instances are here given of this prosperity. <div eID="gen16204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16205" type="x-p"/> 1. Hezekiah shall put off his sackcloth and all the sadness of his countenance, and shall appear publicly in his beauty, in his royal robes and with a pleasing aspect (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.17">v. 17</reference>), to the great joy of all his loving subjects. Those that walk uprightly shall not only have bread given them, and their water sure, but they shall with an eye of faith see the King of kings in his beauty, the beauty of holiness, and that beauty shall be upon them. <div eID="gen16205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16206" type="x-p"/> 2. The siege being raised, by which they were kept close within the walls of Jerusalem, they shall now be at liberty to go abroad upon business or pleasure without danger of falling into the enemies' hand: <hi type="italic">They shall behold the land that is very far off;</hi> they shall visit the utmost corners of the nation, and take a prospect of the adjacent countries, which will be the more pleasant after so long a confinement. Thus believers behold the heavenly Canaan, that land that is very far off, and comfort themselves with the prospect of it in evil times. <div eID="gen16206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16207" type="x-p"/> 3. The remembrance of the fright they were in shall add to the pleasure of their deliverance (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy heart shall meditate terror,</hi> meditate it with pleasure when it is over. Thou shalt think thou still hearest the alarm in thy ears, when all the cry was, "Arm, arm, arm! every man to his post. <hi type="italic">Where is the scribe</hi> or secretary of war? Let him appear to draw up the muster-roll. <hi type="italic">Where is the receiver</hi> and pay-master of the army? Let him see what he had in bank, to defray the charge of a defence. <hi type="italic">Where is he that counted the towers?</hi> Let him bring in the account of them, that care may be taken to put a competent number of men in each." Or these words may be taken as Jerusalem's triumph over the vanquished army of the Assyrians, and the rather because the apostle alludes to them in his triumphs over the learning of this world, when it was baffled by the gospel of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1 Cor. i. 20</reference>. The virgin, the daughter of Zion, despises all their military preparations. Where is the scribe or muster-master of the Assyrian army? Where is their weigher (or treasurer), and where are their engineers that counted the towers? They are all either dead or fled. There is an end of them. <div eID="gen16207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16208" type="x-p"/> 4. They shall no more be terrified with the sight of the Assyrians, who were a fierce people naturally, and were particularly fierce against the people of the Jews, and were of a strange language, that could understand neither their petitions nor their complaints, and therefore had a pretence for being deaf to them, nor could themselves be understood: "They are <hi type="italic">of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive,</hi> which will make them the more formidable, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.19">v. 19</reference>. Thy eyes shall no more see them thus fierce, but their countenances changed when they shall all become dead corpses." <div eID="gen16208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16209" type="x-p"/> 5. They shall no more be under apprehensions of the danger of Jerusalem-Zion, and the temple there (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities,</hi> the city where our solemn sacred feasts are kept, where we used to meet to worship God in religious assemblies." The good people among them, in the time of their distress, were most in pain for Zion upon this account, that it was the city of their solemnities, that the conquerors would burn their temple and they should not have that to keep their solemn feasts in any more. In times of public danger our concern should be most about our religion, and the cities of our solemnities should be dearer to us than either our strong cities or our store-cities. It is with an eye to this that God will work deliverance for Jerusalem, because it is the city of religious solemnities: let those be conscientiously kept up, as the glory of a people, and we may depend upon God to create a defence upon that glory. Two things are here promised to Jerusalem:—(1.) A well-grounded security. It shall be <hi type="italic">a quiet habitation</hi> for the people of God; they shall not be molested and disturbed, as they have been, by the alarms of the sword either of war or persecution, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">ch. xxix. 20</reference>. It shall be a quiet habitation, as it is the city of our solemnities. It is desirable to be quiet in our own houses, but much more so to be quiet in God's house and have none to make us afraid there. Thus it shall be with Jerusalem; and <hi type="italic">the eyes shall see it,</hi> which will be a great satisfaction to a good man, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.5-Ps.128.6">Ps. cxxviii. 5, 6</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt see the good of Jerusalem, and peace upon Israel;</hi> thou shalt live to see it and share in it." (2.) An unmoved stability. Jerusalem, the city of our solemnities, is indeed but <hi type="italic">a tabernacle,</hi> in comparison with the New Jerusalem. The present manifestations of the divine glory and grace are nothing in comparison with those that are reserved for the future state. But it is such a tabernacle as <hi type="italic">shall not be taken down.</hi> After this trouble is over Jerusalem shall long enjoy a confirmed peace; and her sacred privileges, which are the stakes and cords of her tabernacle, shall not be removed from her, nor any disturbance given to the course and circle of her religious services. God's church on earth is a tabernacle, which, though it may be shifted from one place to another, shall not be taken down while the world stands; for in every age Christ will have a seed to serve him. The promises of the covenant are its stakes, which shall never be removed, and the ordinances and institutions of the gospel are its cords, which shall never be broken. They are things which cannot be shaken, though heaven and earth be, but shall remain. <div eID="gen16209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16210" type="x-p"/> 6. God himself will be their protector and Saviour, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21-Isa.33.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. This the principal ground of their confidence: "He that is himself <hi type="italic">the glorious Lord</hi> will display his glory for us and be a glory to us, such as shall eclipse the rival-glory of the enemy." God, in being a gracious Lord, is a glorious Lord; for his goodness is his glory. God will be the Saviour of Jerusalem and her glorious Lord, (1.) As a guard against their adversaries abroad. He will be <hi type="italic">a place of broad rivers and streams.</hi> Jerusalem had no considerable river running by it, as most great cities have, nothing but the brook Kidron, and so wanted one of the best natural fortifications, as well as one of the greatest advantages for trade and commerce, and upon this account their enemies despised them and doubted not but to make an easy prey of them; but the presence and power of God are sufficient at any time to make up to us the deficiencies of the creature and of its strength and beauty. We have all in God, all we need or can desire. Many external advantages Jerusalem has not which other places have, but in God there is more than an equivalent. But, if there be broad rivers and streams about Jerusalem, may not these yield an easy access to the fleet of an invader? No; these are rivers and streams <hi type="italic">in which shall go no galley with oars,</hi> no man of war or gallant ship. If God himself be the river, it must needs be inaccessible to the enemy; they can neither find nor force their way by it. (2.) As a guide to their affairs at home: "<hi type="italic">For the Lord is our Judge,</hi> to whom we are accountable, to whose judgment we refer ourselves, by whose judgment we abide, and who therefore (we hope) will judge for us. <hi type="italic">He is our lawgiver;</hi> his word is a law to us, and to him every thought within us is brought into obedience. <hi type="italic">He is our King,</hi> to whom we pay homage and tribute, and an inviolable allegiance, and therefore <hi type="italic">he will save us.</hi>" For, as protection draws allegiance, so allegiance may expect protection, and shall have it with God. By faith we take Christ for our prince and Saviour, and as such depend upon him and devote ourselves to him. Observe with what an air of triumph, and with what an emphasis laid upon the glorious name of God, they comfort themselves with this: <hi type="italic">Jehovah is our Judge, Jehovah is our Lawgiver, Jehovah is our King, who, being self-existent, is self-sufficient, and all-sufficient to us.</hi> <div eID="gen16210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16211" type="x-p"/> 7. The enemies shall be quite infatuated, and all their powers and projects broken, like a ship at sea in stress of weather, that cannot ride out the storm, but having her tackle torn, her masts split, and nothing wherewith to repair them, is given up for a wreck, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">The tacklings</hi> of the Assyrian <hi type="italic">are loosed;</hi> they are like a ship whose tacklings are loose, or forsaken by the ship's crew, when they give it over for lost, finding that they cannot strengthen the mast, but it will come down. They thought themselves sure of Jerusalem; but when they were just entering the port as it were, and though all was their own, they were quite becalmed, and <hi type="italic">could not spread their sail,</hi> but lay wind-bound till God poured the fury of his wrath upon them. The enemies of God's church are often disarmed and unrigged when they think they have almost gained their point. <div eID="gen16211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16212" type="x-p"/> 8. The wealth of their camp shall be a rich booty for the Jews: <hi type="italic">Then is the prey of a great spoil divided.</hi> When the greater part were slain the rest fled in confusion, and with such precipitation that (like the Syrians) they <hi type="italic">left their tents as they were,</hi> so that all the treasure in them fell into the hands of the besieged; and even <hi type="italic">the lame take the prey.</hi> Those that tarried at home did divide the spoil. It was so easy to come at that not only the strong man might make himself master of it, but even the lame man, whose hands were lame, that he could not fight, and his feet, that he could not pursue. As the victory shall cost them no peril, so the prey shall cost them no toil. And there was such abundance of it that when those who were forward, and came first, had carried off as much as they would, even the lame, who came late, found sufficient. Thus God brought good out of evil, and not only delivered Jerusalem, but enriched it, and abundantly recompensed the losses they had sustained. Thus comfortably and well do the frights and distresses of the people of God often end. <div eID="gen16212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16213" type="x-p"/> 9. Both sickness and sin shall be taken away; and then sickness is taken away in mercy when this is all the fruit of it, and the recovery from it, even the taking away of sin. (1.) <hi type="italic">The inhabitant shall not say, I am sick. As the lame shall take the prey,</hi> so shall the sick, notwithstanding their weakness, make a shift to get to the abandoned camp and seize something for themselves; or there shall be such a universal transport of joy upon this occasion that even the sick shall, for the present, forget their sickness and the sorrows of it, and join with the public in its rejoicings; the deliverance of their city shall be their cure. Or it intimates that, whereas infectious diseases are commonly the effect of long sieges, it shall not be so with Jerusalem, but the inhabitants of it with their victory and peace shall have health also, and there shall be no complaining upon the account of sickness within their gates. Or those that are sick shall bear their sickness without complaining as long as they see it goes well with Jerusalem. Our sense of private grievances should be drowned in our thanksgivings for public mercies. (2.) <hi type="italic">The people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity,</hi> not only the body of the nation forgiven their national guilt in the removing of the national judgment, but particular persons, that dwell therein, shall repent, and reform, and have their sins pardoned. And this is promised as that which is at the bottom of all other favours; he will do so and so for them, <hi type="italic">for he will be merciful to their unrighteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.8.12">Heb. viii. 12</reference>. Sin is the sickness of the soul. When God pardons the sin he heals the disease; and, when the diseases of sin are healed by pardoning mercy, the sting of bodily sickness is taken out and the cause of it removed; so that either the inhabitant shall not be sick or at least shall not say, <hi type="italic">I am sick.</hi> If iniquity be taken away, we have little reason to complain of outward affliction. <hi type="italic">Son, be of good cheer; thy sins are forgiven thee.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.33"/> <div eID="gen16213" type="x-p"/>

entries.6f1bdc54fce8302e587f61d78966a80114c848c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8916"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 33</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.33.1-Isa.33.24">Is 33:1-24</reference>. The Last of Isaiah's Prophecies as to Sennacherib's Overthrow.</title> <div sID="gen14938" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Is 33:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">8, 9</reference>, describe the Assyrian spoiler; strong as he is, he shall fall before Jehovah who is stronger (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.2-Isa.6.10">Is 33:2-6, 10</reference>-12). The time is the autumn of 713 B.C.<div eID="gen14938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8916"/><hi type="bold">1. and thou--</hi>that is, though thou wast not spoiled--though thou wast not dealt treacherously with (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.24.16">Is 24:16</reference>), thy spoiling and treachery are therefore without excuse, being unprovoked.<div eID="gen14939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cease--</hi>When God has let thee do thy worst, in execution of His plans, thine own turn shall come (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Is 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.2">14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">Ha 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Re 13:10</reference>). <div eID="gen14940" type="x-p"/>
entries.877817b5f3fc24701cfc6b8658540e96c063bc22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8917"/><div sID="gen14941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8917"/><hi type="bold">2. us; we ... their ... our--</hi>He speaks interceding for His people, separating himself in thought for a moment from them, and immediately returns to his natural identification with them in the word "our."<div eID="gen14941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every morning--</hi>each day as it dawns, especially during our danger, as the parallel "time of trouble" shows. <div eID="gen14942" type="x-p"/>
entries.069e8188cfd4557755a34f90ff5aa5ad64cd2165: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8918"/><div sID="gen14943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8918"/><hi type="bold">3. the tumult--</hi>the approach of Jehovah is likened to an advancing thunderstorm (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Is 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">30:27</reference>), which is His voice (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.15">Re 1:15</reference>), causing the people to "flee."<div eID="gen14943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nation--</hi>the Assyrian levies. <div eID="gen14944" type="x-p"/>
entries.e39e67657c98629f1a925a9744ff7f55588f1bd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8919"/><div sID="gen14945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8919"/>4. The invaders' "spoil" shall be left behind by them in their flight, and the Jews shall gather it.<div eID="gen14945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">caterpillar--</hi>rather, "the wingless locust"; as it gathers; the Hebrew word for "gathers" is properly used of the gathering of the fruits of harvest (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">Is 32:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">running to and fro--</hi>namely, in gathering harvest fruits.<div eID="gen14947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>rather, "they."<div eID="gen14948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them--</hi>rather, "it," that is, the prey. <div eID="gen14949" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e4c475c197f040db1b37319b1bccf1895f266d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8920"/><div sID="gen14950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8920"/><hi type="bold">6. wisdom--</hi>sacred; that is, piety.<div eID="gen14950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14951" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy--</hi>Hezekiah's; or rather, "Judea's." "His" refers to the same; such changes from the pronoun possessive of the second person to that of the third are common in Hebrew poetry.<div eID="gen14951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treasure--</hi>Not so much material wealth as piety shall constitute the riches of the nation (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.22">Pr 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.16">15:16</reference>). <div eID="gen14952" type="x-p"/>
entries.da566ff42b4066e4cd3252b8ddfacaaa8100dff5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8921"/><div sID="gen14953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8921"/>7-9. From the vision of future glory Isaiah returns to the disastrous present; the grief of "the valiant ones" (parallel to, and identical with, "the ambassadors of peace"), men of rank, sent with presents to sue for peace, but standing "without" the enemy's camp, their suit being rejected (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14">2Ki 18:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.37">18, 37</reference>). The highways deserted through fear, the cities insulted, the lands devastated.<div eID="gen14953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.15.4">Is 15:4</reference>). <div eID="gen14954" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b4695b6bb45440f05a2835218f6801d137a3e91: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8924"/><div sID="gen14962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8924"/>10. The sight of His people's misery arouses Jehovah; He has let the enemy go far enough.<div eID="gen14962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I--</hi>emphatic; God Himself will do what man could not. <div eID="gen14963" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb356c814b5f1c05bd53a2a58b65fc93e98c1708: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8925"/><div sID="gen14964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8925"/><hi type="bold">11. Ye--</hi>the enemy.<div eID="gen14964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">conceive chaff--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.26.18">Is 26:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.4">59:4</reference>).<div eID="gen14965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your breath--</hi>rather, your own spirit of anger and ambition [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.28">Is 30:28</reference>). <div eID="gen14966" type="x-p"/>
entries.86a9e484bcc083f879d414ec55e8b304fe3ffe1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8926"/><div sID="gen14967" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8926"/>12. (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.19">Is 9:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.2.1">Am 2:1</reference>). Perhaps alluding to their being about to be burnt on the funeral pyre (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Is 30:33</reference>).<div eID="gen14967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thorns--</hi>the wicked (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.7">7</reference>). <div eID="gen14968" type="x-p"/>
entries.991b590d7e5714414b7f93352188c0fc9744729c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8927"/><div sID="gen14969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8927"/><hi type="bold">13. far off--</hi>distant nations.<div eID="gen14969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">near--</hi>the Jews and adjoining peoples (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">Is 49:1</reference>). <div eID="gen14970" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe3e69536980b20c9340e3fb046c8fc4ac32c4c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8928"/><div sID="gen14971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8928"/><hi type="bold">14. sinners in Zion--</hi>false professors of religion among the elect people (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.12">Mt 22:12</reference>).<div eID="gen14971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14972" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hypocrites--</hi>rather, "the profane"; "the abandoned" [Horsley].<div eID="gen14972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who, &c.--</hi>If Jehovah's wrath could thus consume such a host in one night, who could abide it, if continued for ever (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.46-Mark.9.48">Mr 9:46-48</reference>)? Fire is a common image for the divine judgments (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Is 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">30:30</reference>).<div eID="gen14973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among us--</hi>If such awful judgments have fallen on those who knew not the true God, how infinitely worse shall fall on us who, amid religious privileges and profession, sin against God, (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.47">Lu 12:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.48">48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.17">Jas 4:17</reference>)? <div eID="gen14974" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf91cf1f580a510306bb209fcb8fb0bbe70f3c12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8929"/><div sID="gen14975" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8929"/>15. In contrast to the trembling "sinners in Zion" (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Is 33:14</reference>), the righteous shall be secure amid all judgments; they are described according to the Old Testament standpoint of righteousness (<reference osisRef="Ps.15.2">Psa 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">24:4</reference>).<div eID="gen14975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stoppeth ... ears ... eyes--</hi>"Rejoiceth not in iniquity" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.6">1Co 13:6</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">Is 29:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Psa 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.32">Ro 1:32</reference>). The senses are avenues for the entrance of sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.37">Psa 119:37</reference>). <div eID="gen14976" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb7d29556f95c5756e8bd74bd096e26a438a9eaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8930"/><div sID="gen14977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8930"/><hi type="bold">16. on high--</hi>heights inaccessible to the foe (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Is 26:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bread ... waters--</hi>image from the expected siege by Sennacherib; however besieged by trials without, the godly shall have literal and spiritual food, as God sees good for them (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.17">Is 41:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">Psa 37:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.10">34:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.15">132:15</reference>). <div eID="gen14978" type="x-p"/>
entries.55f73245414374fa37cb9a2eb86ee71843ff0bcb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8931"/><div sID="gen14979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8931"/><hi type="bold">17. Thine--</hi>the saints'.<div eID="gen14979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king in ... beauty--</hi>not as now, Hezekiah in sackcloth, oppressed by the enemy, but King Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Is 32:1</reference>) "in His beauty" (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.5.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.3">Re 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen14980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land ... very far off--</hi>rather, "the land in its remotest extent" (no longer pent up as Hezekiah was with the siege); see Margin. For Jerusalem is made the scene of the king's glory (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">Is 33:20</reference>, &c.), and it could not be said to be "very far off," unless the far-off land be heaven, the Jerusalem above, which is to follow the earthly reign of Messiah at literal Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.17-Isa.65.19">Is 65:17-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>, 2, 10). <div eID="gen14981" type="x-p"/>
entries.92716d139ca9eee04ab5801540cca39b279943c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8932"/><div sID="gen14982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8932"/><hi type="bold">18. meditate--</hi>on the "terror" caused by the enemy, but now past.<div eID="gen14982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">where, &c.--</hi>the language of the Jews exulting over their escape from danger.<div eID="gen14983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scribe--</hi>who enrolled the army [Maurer]; or, who prescribed the tribute to be paid [Rosenmuller]; or, who kept an account of the spoil. "The principal scribe of the host" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.19">2Ki 25:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.25">Jr 52:25</reference>). The Assyrian records are free from the exaggerations of Egyptian records. Two scribes are seen in every Assyrian bas-relief, writing down the various objects brought to them, the heads of the slain, prisoners, cattle, sheep, &c.<div eID="gen14984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receiver--</hi>"weigher," Margin. Layard mentions, among the Assyrian inscriptions, "a pair a scales for weighing the spoils."<div eID="gen14985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14986" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counted ... towers--</hi>he whose duty it was to reconnoitre and report the strength of the city to be besieged. <div eID="gen14986" type="x-p"/>
entries.096a4e1a29503630011c399dc24f5bf03ce2a38c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8933"/><div sID="gen14987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8933"/><hi type="bold">19. fierce people--</hi>The Assyrians shall not be allowed to enter Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.32">2Ki 19:32</reference>). Or, thou shalt not any longer see fierce enemies threatening thee as previously; such as the Assyrians, Romans, and the last Antichristian host that is yet to assail Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">De 28:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.50">50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.15">Jr 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">Zec 14:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stammering--</hi>barbarous; so "deeper," &c., that is, unintelligible. The Assyrian tongue differed only in dialect from the Hebrew, but in the Assyrian levies were many of non-Semitic race and language, as the Medes, Elamites, &c. (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.28.11">Is 28:11</reference>). <div eID="gen14988" type="x-p"/>
entries.19dfc87a46d588f0199d9bd310ae7be21cd7d692: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8934"/><div sID="gen14989" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8934"/><hi type="bold">20. solemnities--</hi>solemn assemblies at the great feasts (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Is 30:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Psa 42:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.12">Psa 48:12</reference>).<div eID="gen14989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... taken down ... removed--</hi>image from captives "removed" from their land (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.17">Is 36:17</reference>). There shall be no more "taking away" to an enemy's land. Or else, from nomads living in shifting tents. The saints, who sojourned once in tabernacles as pilgrims, shall have a "building of God--eternal in the heavens" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.9">He 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.10">10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.54.2">Is 54:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stakes--</hi>driven into the ground; to these the "cords" were fastened. Christ's Church shall never fall (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>). So individual believers (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen14991" type="x-p"/>
entries.29184b63ed71bf9e2a4955404f7d1ee6ad02ed41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8935"/><div sID="gen14992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8935"/><hi type="bold">21. there--</hi>namely, in Jerusalem.<div eID="gen14992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14993" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will be ... rivers--</hi>Jehovah will be as a broad river surrounding our city (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.19.6">Is 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Na 3:8</reference>), and this, too, a river of such a kind as no ship of war can pass (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Is 26:1</reference>). Jerusalem had not the advantage of a river; Jehovah will be as one to it, affording all the advantages, without any of the disadvantages of one.<div eID="gen14993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">galley with oars--</hi>war vessels of a long shape, and propelled by oars; merchant vessels were broader and carried sail.<div eID="gen14994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14995" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gallant--</hi>same Hebrew word as for "glorious," previously; "mighty" will suit both places; a ship of war is meant. No "mighty vessel" will dare to pass where the "mighty Lord" stands as our defense. <div eID="gen14995" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ea25ada14e4fc82941f3efec15ce1daaee3064b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8936"/><div sID="gen14996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8936"/><hi type="bold">22. Lord--</hi>thrice repeated, as often: the Trinity (<reference osisRef="Num.6.24-Num.6.26">Nu 6:24-26</reference>).<div eID="gen14996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judge ... lawgiver ... king--</hi>perfect ideal of the theocracy, to be realized under Messiah alone; the judicial, legislative, and administrative functions as king to be exercised by Him in person (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.12">Jas 4:12</reference>). <div eID="gen14997" type="x-p"/>
entries.a93acf4c0cda0645023e5db0933a2419319bce3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8937"/><div sID="gen14998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8937"/><hi type="bold">23. tacklings--</hi>Continuing the allegory in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Is 33:21</reference>, he compares the enemies' host to a war galley which is deprived of the tacklings or cords by which the mast is sustained and the sail is spread; and which therefore is sure to be wrecked on "the broad river" (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Is 33:21</reference>), and become the prey of Israel.<div eID="gen14998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they--</hi>the tacklings, "hold not firm the base of the mast."<div eID="gen14999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>when the Assyrian host shall have been discomfited. Hezekiah had given Sennacherib three hundred talents of silver, and thirty of gold (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14-2Kgs.18.16">2Ki 18:14-16</reference>), and had stripped the temple of its gold to give it to him; this treasure was probably part of the prey found in the foe's camp. After the invasion, Hezekiah had so much wealth that he made an improper display of it (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.13-2Kgs.20.15">2Ki 20:13-15</reference>); this wealth, probably, was in part got from the Assyrian.<div eID="gen15000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the lame--</hi>Even the most feeble shall spoil the Assyrian camp (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.35.6">Is 35:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6">2Sa 5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen15001" type="x-p"/>
entries.d94f959ae48597ba14752c1285843f8b03560ee1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8938"/><div sID="gen15002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8938"/><hi type="bold">24. sick--</hi>Smith thinks the allusion is to the beginning of the pestilence by which the Assyrians were destroyed, and which, while sparing the righteous, affected some within the city ("sinners in Zion"); it may have been the sickness that visited Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.1-Isa.38.22">Is 38:1-22</reference>). In the Jerusalem to come there shall be no "sickness," because there will be no "iniquity," it being forgiven (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>). The latter clause of the verse contains the cause of the former (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.5-Mark.2.9">Mr 2:5-9</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.33"/>

entries.1a59239766ccd85a35b4e01b7bcc27bb27b28466: <div eID="gen27840" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27841" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27842" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27842" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27841" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27843" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains the sequel of the prophecy respecting Sennacherib. The prophet addresses himself to the Assyrian monarch, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1-Isa.33.4">Isa 33:1-4</reference>. The mercy and power of God acknowledged by the Jews, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">Isa 33:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.6">Isa 33:6</reference>. Distress and despair of the Jews at the approach of Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.7-Isa.33.9">Isa 33:7-9</reference>. Gracious promise of deliverance, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10-Isa.33.13">Isa 33:10-13</reference>. Dreadful apprehensions of the wicked, and security of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14-Isa.33.17">Isa 33:14-17</reference>. The security of the Jews under the reign of Hezekiah, and the wretched condition of Sennacherib and his army, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.18-Isa.33.24">Isa 33:18-24</reference>. <div eID="gen27843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27844" type="x-p"/> The plan of the prophecy continued in this chapter, and which is manifestly distinct from the foregoing, is peculiarly elegant. To set it in a proper light, it will be necessary to mark the transitions from one part of it to another. <div eID="gen27844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27845" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>, the prophet addresses himself to Sennacherib, briefly, but strongly and elegantly, expressing the injustice of his ambitious designs, and the sudden disappointments of them. <div eID="gen27845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27846" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa 33:2</reference>, the Jews are introduced offering up their earnest supplications to God in their present distressful condition; with expressions of their trust and confidence in his protection. <div eID="gen27846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27847" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">Isa 33:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">Isa 33:4</reference> the prophet in the name of God, or rather God himself, is introduced addressing himself to Sennacherib, and threatening him that, notwithstanding the terror which he had occasioned in the invaded countries, yet he should fall, and become an easy prey to those whom he had intended to subdue. <div eID="gen27847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27848" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">Isa 33:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.33.6">Isa 33:6</reference>, a chorus of Jews is introduced, acknowledging the mercy and power of God, who had undertaken to protect them; extolling it with direct opposition to the boasted power of their enemies, and celebrating the wisdom and piety of their king Hezekiah, who had placed his confidence in the favor of God. <div eID="gen27848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27849" type="x-p"/> Then follows, in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.7">Isa 33:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.8">Isa 33:8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">Isa 33:9</reference>, a description of the distress and despair of the Jews, upon the king of Assyria's marching against Jerusalem, and sending his summons to them to surrender, after the treaty he had made with Hezekiah on the conditions of his paying, as he actually did pay to him, three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14-2Kgs.18.16">2Kgs 18:14-16</reference>. <div eID="gen27849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27850" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10">Isa 33:10</reference>, God himself is again introduced, declaring that he will interpose in this critical situation of affairs, and disappoint the vain designs of the enemies of his people, by discomfiting and utterly consuming them. <div eID="gen27850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27851" type="x-p"/> Then follows, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.11-Isa.33.22">Isa 33:11-22</reference>, still in the person of God, which however falls at last into that of the prophet, a description of the dreadful apprehensions of the wicked in those times of distress and imminent danger; finely contrasted with the confidence and security of the righteous, and their trust in the promises of God that he will be their never-failing strength and protector. <div eID="gen27851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27852" type="x-p"/> The whole concludes, in the person of the prophet, with a description of the security of the Jews under the protection of God, and of the wretched state of Sennacherib and his army, wholly discomfited, and exposed to be plundered even by the weakest of the enemy. <div eID="gen27852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27853" type="x-p"/> Much of the beauty of this passage depends on the explanation above given of <reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">Isa 33:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">Isa 33:4</reference>, as addressed by the prophet, or by God himself, to Sennacherib; not as it is usually taken, as addressed by the Jews to God, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">Isa 33:3</reference>, and then <reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">Isa 33:4</reference>, as addressed to the Assyrians. To set this in a clear light, it may be of use to compare it with a passage of the Prophet Joel; where, speaking of the destruction caused by the locusts, he sets in the same strong light of opposition as Isaiah does here, the power of the enemy, and the power of Jehovah, who would destroy that enemy. Thus Isaiah to Sennacherib: - "When thou didst raise thyself up, the nations were dispersed" - <reference osisRef="Isa.33.3">Isa 33:3</reference>. "But now will I arise, saith Jehovah; Now will I be exalted." <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10">Isa 33:10</reference>. <div eID="gen27853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27854" type="x-p"/> And thus Joel, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.20">Joe 2:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.21">Joe 2:21</reference> : - "His stink shall come up, and his ill savor shall ascend; Though he hath done great things. Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice; For Jehovah will do great things." - L. <div eID="gen27854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27855" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27856" type="x-p"/> And deadest treacherously "Thou plunderer" - See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Isa 21:2</reference> (note). <div eID="gen27856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27857" type="x-p"/> When thou shalt make an end to deal treacherously "When thou art weary of plundering" - "כנלתך cannelothecha, alibi non extat in s. s. nisi f. <reference osisRef="Job.15.29">Job 15:29</reference> - simplicius est legere ככלתך kechallothecha. Vid. Capell.; nec repugnat Vitringa. Vid. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan 9:24</reference>. כלה calah התים hatim." - Secker.
entries.8bd2b7b21c13635cf0c6bc3effbd70ced51282cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27858" type="x-p"/> Be thou their arm every morning "Be thou our strength every morning" - For זרעם zeroam, their arm, the Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate read זרענו zeroenu, our arm, in the first person of the pronoun, not the third: the edition of Felix Pratensis has זרעתינו zerootheynu in the margin. <div eID="gen27858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27859" type="x-p"/> The prophet is here praying against the enemies of God's people; and yet this part of the prayer seems to be in their behalf: but from the above authorities it appears that Our arm is the true reading, though I do not find it confirmed by any of Kennicott's, De Rossi's, or my own MSS. My old MS. Bible has, - Be thou oure arm in erly.
entries.9d898fbb4f13b40714ca5c5f356651faa9d14886: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27860" type="x-p"/> At the noise of the tumult "From thy terrible voice" - For המון hamon, "multitude," the Septuagint and Syriac read אמיך amica, "terrible," whom I follow.
entries.229b792a32adf79bb73f8b521743a4a4dbcc27d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27861" type="x-p"/> His treasure "Thy treasure" - Ὁ θησαυρος σου, Sym. He had in his copy אצרך otsarcha, "thy treasure, "not אצרו otsaro, "his treasure."
entries.a36961d514d50c6026cd92a9468ebc9fd17bb9e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27862" type="x-p"/> Their valiant ones shall cry without "The mighty men raise a grievous cry" - Three MSS. read אראלים erelim, that is, lions of God, or strong lions. So they called valiant men heroes; which appellation the Arabians and Persians still use. See Bochart. Hieroz. Part 1 lib. 3 cap. 1. "Mahomet, ayant reconnu Hamzeh son oncle pour homme de courage et de valeur, lui donne le titre ou surnom d'Assad Allah, qui signifie le lion de Dieu. "D'Herbelot, p. 427. And for חצה chatsah, the Syriac and Chaldee, read קשה kashah, whom I follow. The Chaldee, Syriac, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion read אראה להם ereh lahem, or יראה yireh, with what meaning is not clear. <div eID="gen27862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27863" type="x-p"/> The word אראלם erellam, which we translate valiant ones, is very difficult; no man knows what it means. Kimchi supposes that it is the name of the angel that smote the Assyrian camp! The Vulgate, and my old MS., translate it seers; and most of the Versions understand it in this way. None of the MSS. give us any help, but as we see above in Lowth.
entries.d35c8a33acf51f0a7452aa57ac131d2e7c3b014f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27864" type="x-p"/> Bashan and Carmel shake off their fruits "Bashan and Carmel are stripped of their beauty" - Φανερα εσται, made manifest. Sept. They read ונערה veneerah.
entries.41692116ee07bf8f1d6af51b00ab5e6274261318: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27865" type="x-p"/> Your breath "And my spirit" - "For רוחכם ruchechem, your spirit, read רוחי כמו ruchi kemo. "Secker. Which reading is confirmed by the Chaldee, where מימרי meymri, "my word, "answers to רוחי ruchi, "my spirit."
entries.c7c928c3a03efd147a680d227e6863f1cfd085fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27866" type="x-p"/> The sinners in Zion are afraid - Zion has been generally considered as a type of the Church of God. Now all the members of God's Church should be holy, and given to good works; sinners in Zion, therefore, are portentous beings! but, alas! where are they not? The Targum on this verse is worthy of notice: "The sinners in Zion are broken down; fear hath seized the ungodly, who are suffering for their ways. They say, Who among us shall dwell in Zion, where the splendor of the Divine Majesty is like a consuming fire? Who of us shall dwell in Jerusalem, where the ungodly are judged and delivered into hell for an eternal burning?" Everdurynge brennyngis. Old MS. Bible.
entries.b9eed5d6227e9329fe03feaa2a25d1d604d4c005: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27867" type="x-p"/> That stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood "Who stoppeth his ears to the proposal of bloodshed" - A MS. reads בדמים bedamim, "in blood."
